sentences.text: This streamlined predator fed on other bony fish and grew from roughly 50 cm to a maximum of 2.5 meters in length.
Its rounded scales and body shape suggest it could swim quickly to catch prey.
Like other rhipidistians, it possessed fang-like teeth on its palate and smaller teeth on its jaws.
An asymmetrical tail with a caudal fin located on the lower end required its pectoral fins to be positioned high on the body to counteract the downward push.
Isotopic analysis of remains from Greenland suggests this organism was likely euryhaline, capable of living in varying salinities.
One valid species, H. bergmanni, is known from Frasnian fossils found in Ellesmere Island, Arctic Canada.
The genus Holoptychius was first described by Louis Agassiz in 1839.
The species H. jarviki was previously often called H. quebecensis before being described as a distinct species in 1996 after its material was separated from Quebecius quebecensis.
Researchers suggest Holoptychius was likely an ambush predator with a lifestyle similar to the modern arapaima.
H. nobilissimus is the type species of Holoptychius, found in Late Frasnian to early Famennian rocks in Scotland, England, Latvia, Norway, and Russia.
The genus Glytolepis was formerly treated as a subgenus of Holoptychius.
Fossils of Holoptychius have been found worldwide, including North America, South America, and much of Europe.
Holoptychius fossils have been discovered in Belgium, Colombia, Norway, Canada, Russia, Greenland, and the United States.
